items.title: Predicting Seed Variance, Warmup & LR Decay | Stanford CS312 Quiz Review with Suhas Kotha
items.summary:
Browse Stanford's online courses in deep learning: https://stanford.io/4zhLWFN

How much does validation loss move between random seeds, and how long should learning rate warmup and decay last? In this Stanford CS312: Deep Learning Alchemy quiz review, PhD student Suhas Kotha walks through the answers to held-out experiments on the d8 language model, covering run-to-run variance, training loss jitter and batch size, warmup and WSD decay schedules, parameter and gradient norms under weight decay, and scaling-law extrapolation. Each answer comes with instructor sweeps, related papers, and the mental model updates it supports.

Key questions answered in this lecture:
Q: How much does validation loss vary between random seeds in LLM pretraining?
A: In this setup the run-to-run standard deviation is about 0.003 validation loss, and varying only the initialization seed or only the data seed gives nearly all of that variance. Differences near 0.003 are noise; something like 0.02 is likely a real improvement.

Q: How does training loss noise change with batch size?
A: Train-loss jitter scales roughly as 1 over the square root of batch size, because it is dominated by sampling variance of the batch, not the model; it barely changes with learning rate. Validation loss has far less jitter, so it is the cleaner measurement.

Q: How long should the decay phase of a WSD learning rate schedule be?
A: To get within 0.02 loss of the best schedule, the cooldown needed to be around 20% of training in this setting. Kotha notes these are not fixed constants and depend on what you train on.

Q: How does learning rate warmup affect the optimal learning rate?
A: Longer warmup raises the optimal learning rate and tolerance to high learning rates: about 1e-3 to 2e-3 with almost no warmup vs closer to 5e-3 with 30% warmup. The best warmup here was 20-30%, far above the 1% default, and it shrinks at longer token horizons, suggesting warmup should be a fixed number of steps.

Q: Why does parameter norm grow during transformer training and what stops it?
A: With layer norm the loss does not care about weight scale, so gradient updates are mostly orthogonal to the weights and the norm drifts upward. Lower learning rates slow the drift and weight decay pulls it back; only the combination of weight decay and a linear decay schedule made the norm start decreasing.

Q: Can small-model scaling laws predict which method wins at larger scale?
A: Fitting on D4 through D9 got the ranking right and predicted that dropout, worse at small sizes, would win at larger parameter counts. Kotha warns that a fit that looks good on all points is no guarantee for further extrapolation.

items.title: Better Data for AI Agents: Data Selection & Quality | Stanford CS329Z Lecture 11 with John Yang
items.summary:
Browse Stanford's online courses in Agentic AI: https://stanford.io/4AIRb2z

You have millions of agent trajectories. Which ones should you train on? In this Stanford CS329Z: Engineering AI Agents lecture, John Yang, co-creator of SWE-bench and SWE-smith, explains how to find maximally informative data: filtering and selection strategies for validity and learnability, tiny-but-targeted benchmarks, annotation practices (including how SWE-bench Verified was built), quality assessment and automated checks for coding tasks, curricula for reinforcement learning, building datasets from agent traces (including failed trajectories), and when less but better data beats more data.

Key questions answered in this lecture:
Q: Should you fine-tune agents only on successful trajectories?
A: No. Keeping only successes biases data toward what the teacher model can already solve. Failed trajectories, labeled or corrected, improve results.

Q: What makes a reinforcement learning task learnable?
A: The model should succeed sometimes but not always (for example, 1 to 7 times out of 8 rollouts), so there is a useful learning signal. Re-filter as the model improves.

Q: How was SWE-bench Verified created?
A: Professional developers annotated about 1,700 SWE-bench tasks for problems like underspecified issues and unfair tests, and the curated result is 500 tasks.

Q: How do you automatically filter coding tasks?
A: Run the reference solution several times to remove flaky tests, confirm the starting state fails, flag hard-coded expectations, and use an LLM monitor to catch leakage and reward hacking.

Q: Is more data or better data better for agents?
A: “More better data” is best, but under a fixed compute budget or for a specialist agent, a small curated dataset can match a much larger one.

items.title: What Data Do AI Agents Need? | Stanford CS329Z Lecture 10 with John Yang
items.summary:
Browse Stanford's online courses in Agentic AI: https://stanford.io/4AIRb2z

Where does the training data for AI agents come from? In this Stanford CS329Z: Engineering AI Agents lecture, John Yang, co-creator of SWE-bench and SWE-agent, explains what data agents need (traces, demonstrations, and feedback), data for optimization vs. evaluation, data flywheels, and why agents need environments and not just web text. He covers the difference between trajectories and environments, how to verify agent work, and strategies for collecting agent data: human demonstrations, mining the web, synthetic data generation (LLM-synthesized trajectories and tasks like SWE-smith and R2E-Gym), simulated users, and collecting data from human-agent interaction. He also covers pitfalls like reward hacking and overfitting.

Key questions answered in this lecture:
Q: Why do AI agents need environments if the web already has the knowledge?
A: The internet is like a textbook and an environment is the lab. Pretraining on code teaches what code looks like, not how to run it, read the output, and iterate.

Q: What is the difference between an agent trajectory and an environment?
A: A trajectory is a log of thought-action-observation steps used for supervised fine-tuning. An environment has a task, an action space, and verification, and is used for reinforcement learning.

Q: How is training data for AI agents collected?
A: Five main ways: human demonstrations, mining web artifacts like GitHub PRs and tutorials, LLM-synthesized trajectories, synthesized tasks, and simulated users or environments.

Q: How does SWE-smith create software engineering training tasks?
A: Instead of mining scarce real PRs, it takes a working repository and deliberately introduces bugs so tests fail reliably, scaling to 50,000 tasks.

Q: What goes wrong when you train agents on this data?
A: Reward hacking (like checking out the future fixed commit), benchmark memorization, overfitting to a single harness, and degradation from too much SFT data.

items.title: Hyperparameter Tuning, Scaling Laws & Debugging | Stanford CS312 Lecture 2 with Tatsunori Hashimoto
items.summary:
Browse Stanford's online courses in deep learning: https://stanford.io/4zhLWFN

Why do so many claimed wins in deep learning disappear once you tune the baseline? In this Stanford CS312: Deep Learning Alchemy lecture, Assistant Professor Tatsunori Hashimoto covers four basic experimental skills: hyperparameters, scaling laws, stochasticity, and debugging. He shows how untuned learning rates produced false results, how Step Law sweeps link learning rate and batch size, why scaling laws are engineered and can break at the largest run, why training behaves like a chaotic system, and how to debug a network by comparing it to a known good control.

Key questions answered in this lecture:
Q: What is the most important hyperparameter to tune in deep learning?
A: Hashimoto says if you can only tune one thing, tune the learning rate; there is no theoretical reason, but it is the most sensitive. Others like Adam momentum usually matter little, and model size or step count are usually held fixed to keep compute constant.

Q: Do new optimizers like Lion or MARS beat AdamW?
A: Many claimed wins come from poorly tuned AdamW baselines. Retuning the learning rate makes AdamW match MARS, and with optimally tuned weight decay, AdamW beats Lion.

Q: How do optimal learning rate and batch size change with model size and data?
A: In the StepFun Step Law sweeps, loss is roughly quadratic in log learning rate and batch size, and the two are correlated. Both optima shift with scale, so in the worst case you must retune for every model, which is why small-scale tuning and transfer matter.

Q: Why do scaling laws sometimes fail to predict large training runs?
A: Hashimoto says scaling laws are engineered through a lot of pain: a fit that looks perfect can blow up at the largest run, as in Marin, and choices like hyperparameter scaling and how you count parameters or FLOPs (part of the Kaplan vs. Chinchilla disagreement) shift the fits.

Q: Where does randomness in neural network training come from?
A: Data order, initialization, and augmentation each produce about the same final variance, and turning all on barely adds more. Even tiny perturbations amplify like a chaotic system, so training is effectively stochastic even when deterministic.

Q: How do I debug a neural network that will not train?
A: Know what normal looks like, track internal statistics like activations, gradients, and attention logits against a known good control, and understand invariances such as layer norm. Change one thing at a time and interpolate between the working model and the broken one.

items.title: Are You Psychic? What a P-Value Can't Predict | Kristin Sainani & Regina Nuzzo
items.summary:
Enrollment is now open!

🔗https://stanford.io/som-xche0033

Graduate Winter Quarter
🔗https://stanford.io/Winter-2026

What does a p-value tell you? Stanford's Kristin Sainani and Regina Nuzzo, two statistics professors and science journalists, explain p-values with a mind-reading experiment instead of the technical definition. 

Nuzzo thinks of a number between 1 and 20, Sainani guesses until she is right, and the pair calculate the p-value for her six tries. The result is 30%, which means that guessing alone would produce a result at least this good 30% of the time. 

Sainani explains why that is not impressive evidence of psychic ability, and why the most common mistake is to read a p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, or that chance alone is at work. In this video, Sainani says many scientists get this wrong, and Nuzzo explains why a p-value cannot tell you the chance that someone is psychic.

Key questions answered in this video:
Q: What is a p-value in simple terms?
A: The video defines it as the probability of observing your result, or results even more surprising, if the null hypothesis is true. In the guessing experiment, a 30% p-value means she would have had a 30% chance of getting the right answer in six or fewer tries by guessing.
Q: What is a null hypothesis?
A: Nuzzo explains that in the experiment, the null hypothesis is that Sainani is not psychic and is just guessing.
Q: What does a small p-value mean?
A: The smaller the p-value, the more evidence against the null hypothesis. If it were small enough, they could reject the null hypothesis and conclude that Sainani is psychic.
Q: What is the biggest mistake people make when interpreting p-values?
A: People mistakenly treat the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, or that chance is at work. Here, that would imply a 70% chance that Sainani is psychic, which is clearly wrong.

Regina Nuzzo is a freelance science writer and professor in Washington, DC. She earned her PhD in Statistics from Stanford and teaches statistics in American Sign Language at Gallaudet University.

items.title: Deep Learning by Prediction: Intro | Stanford CS312 Lecture 1 with Tatsunori Hashimoto & Suhas Kotha
items.summary:
Browse Stanford's online courses in deep learning: https://stanford.io/4zhLWFN

Can you predict the result of a deep learning experiment before you run it? In this Stanford CS312: Deep Learning Alchemy lecture, Assistant Professor Tatsunori Hashimoto and PhD student Suhas Kotha introduce the idea at the heart of the class: prediction as understanding. Hashimoto explains why classical intuitions like the bias-variance tradeoff mislead deep learning practitioners and why the class embraces the alchemy through experiments and prediction quizzes. Kotha then lays out the pre-training setting and the d8 model organism, a 30M-parameter, 8-layer transformer that trains in about ten minutes on one GPU, with a live learning rate sweep and architecture ablations.

Key questions answered in this lecture:
Q: Why is the bias-variance tradeoff the wrong mental model for deep learning?
A: Hashimoto says networks with more parameters than data generalize anyway, and even double descent is brittle: with well-tuned hyperparameters and regularization, the curve often looks like a single descent. Classical models lead to nonsensical design choices.

Q: How does Stanford CS312 teach deep learning with prediction quizzes?
A: In the class, Stanford students run experiments in assignments and then take quizzes asking them to predict the outcome of a held-out experiment, given as a runnable code diff. The goal is to build an internal world model of deep learning, the way science used prediction before it had theory.

Q: Why are CS312 assignments worth 0% of the grade?
A: Grading heavy assignments penalized students who did not lean on Claude Code, so assignments are ungraded and AI use is permitted. Students are motivated because assignments are quiz prep and are the only way to earn partial credit, up to 75%, by citing their own experiments.

Q: Why study pre-training instead of fine-tuning or RL to learn deep learning?
A: Suhas Kotha says pre-training has a low-noise validation loss that predicts downstream ability, scaling laws let small runs reflect large ones, and every run starts from random weights, so experiments are reproducible and easy to reason about.

Q: What is the d8 model used in CS312?
A: A Llama-style 8-layer transformer with about 30 million parameters, trained on about 600 million tokens of web text with a 4096-token vocabulary and 1024-token sequences. One run takes about ten minutes on a single GPU and reaches about 2.93 loss at the default learning rate of 3e-3.

Q: What happens if you remove residual connections or prenorm from a transformer?
A: In the d8 ablations, removing residuals made essentially nothing train, while attention mattered much more than the MLP. Removing prenorm only looked fatal at the default learning rate; with a 3x lower learning rate, it trained close to the other variants.

Can working professionals take Stanford graduate-level engineering classes without committing to a full degree? In this Stanford Online information session, Pax Heymeyer, Senior Director of Academic Programs, and Jonathan Nottman, Senior Director of Client Success and Engagement, explain three paths: taking individual graduate courses for credit, earning a graduate certificate, or pursuing a part-time master's degree with the option to study online.

The Stanford Engineering Center for Global and Online Education traces its history to 1954, when it began as a way for employees of Stanford Research Park companies to study part-time. Professionals with a bachelor's degree can apply as non-degree students for individual courses and graduate certificates.

Applicants submit official transcripts, identification, and a short statement of purpose, but no letters of recommendation. The academic department reviews each application when the student enrolls in a course, and students must earn a B or better to continue. A graduate certificate takes three to four courses, usually within three years, and up to 18 units from non-degree courses can count toward a Stanford master's degree with department approval.

Key questions answered in this session:
Q: Who can take Stanford graduate courses as a non-degree student?
A: Professionals with a bachelor's degree who meet department prerequisites and submit official transcripts. No letters of recommendation are required.
Q: How much time should I plan for each week?
A: 15 to 25 hours of coursework per week in a 10-week quarter.
Q: Do I have to take exams in person?
A: Most exams are taken in person at an approved proctor, such as a testing center or a supervisor, usually within a window of at least 24 hours.
Q: Can non-degree units count toward a master's degree?
A: Up to 18 units can transfer to a master's degree with department approval. They cannot be applied to a graduate certificate.
Q: Are the programs available outside the U.S.?
A: Yes. They are open to students worldwide.
Q: Does doing well in these classes help master's admission?
A: It helps, because it shows graduate-level performance, but it does not guarantee admission.

About the speakers:
Pax Heymeyer is Senior Director of Academic Programs at the Stanford Engineering Center for Global and Online Education. Jonathan Nottman is Senior Director of Client Success and Engagement.

items.title: AI Costs: Tokens, Energy, Model Choice & API Keys | Stanford CS193T Lecture 7 with Cynthia Bailey
items.summary:
Explore AI courses and programs from Stanford Online: https://stanford.io/4BYTekh 

What does it cost to use AI in tokens, dollars, electricity, and water? In this Stanford CS193T: Thinking with AI lecture recording, Senior Lecturer Cynthia Bailey reads a real Claude Code usage report line by line, shows how caching saves money by reusing attention-mechanism calculations, and reviews estimates of AI's electricity and water use and how they vary by task and context size. She then covers model selection, including why bigger is not always better once latency compounds across a multi-step agentic workflow, and API keys: what they are, why they matter for billing and security, and a hands-on demonstration of how one leaks. The lecture closes with a current-events look at how the real-world costs of AI became a factor in the 2026 midterm elections.

Key questions answered in this lecture:
Q: What do the numbers in a Claude Code usage report mean?
A: Bailey walks through total cost, API duration (time spent waiting on the model, including network transit and data center load), wall-clock time since the session began, and input versus output tokens. Input tokens cover everything the model reads, including the system prompt, settings, and connectors. Output tokens include the model's reasoning.

Q: How does caching reduce the cost of using an AI model?
A: Much of the context window repeats from prompt to prompt, so a precomputed version is saved instead of being reprocessed. Because the attention calculation is done once and reused, cache reads can be discounted by up to about 90% compared with raw input tokens.

Q: Do unused skills still add to token costs?
A: Yes. Every enabled skill places its text in the context window on each prompt, so unused skills still add cost. Bailey recommends removing skills an agent does not need and starting a fresh session when you switch tasks.

Q: How much electricity and water does an AI prompt use?
A: Bailey cites Google's self-reported 2025 figures for a median Gemini text prompt, about 0.26 mL of water and 0.24 Wh of electricity, and notes that public data is limited. She also covers research estimates that image generation costs 20 to 40 times more than text and video 1,000 to 3,000 times more, with reasoning modes averaging about 30 times more.

Q: How should you choose a model for an AI agent?
A: Bigger is not automatically better, because larger models bring higher latency, and that delay repeats at every step of a multi-agent workflow. A narrow check against an objective rule can suit the smallest, cheapest model, while a guardrail that must interpret policy with nuance calls for a stronger one.

Q: What is an API key, and how can one leak?
A: An API key works like login credentials for a program, letting it call an AI model and bill the usage to your account, so it deserves the same care as a password. If a key is written into a web page's code, anyone can view the page source, copy it and run up charges, so it must be kept out of public view.

Is making a model bigger still the only way to improve it? Adjunct Professors Afshine Amidi and Shervine Amidi explain how post-training techniques such as finetuning, reinforcement learning, preference optimization, verifier-guided training, and distillation help a model reason better, follow instructions better, solve harder problems, and adapt to specialized domains.

They then focus on on-policy distillation. In standard distillation, a smaller student model learns from examples produced by a stronger teacher. In on-policy distillation, the student generates its own responses during training and learns from how the teacher evaluates those exact attempts. According to the Amidi brothers, this aligns the learning process with how the model behaves in practice, which matters most for reasoning tasks, where intermediate steps, mistakes, and corrections shape the result.

Will AI replace statisticians? Stanford's Kristin Sainani and Regina Nuzzo, two statistics professors and science journalists, say the field is more important than ever. In this conversation, they discuss how large language models (LLMs) can improve statistical practice, why linear models and machine learning have roots in statistics, and why a human needs to stay in the middle of any AI-assisted analysis. Sainani is excited about LLMs helping people who analyze their own data without a statistician. Nuzzo argues that statisticians understand both how machines work and how humans think, which is the point where AI needs oversight.

Key questions answered in this video:
Q: Do we still need statisticians in the age of AI and LLMs?
A: Yes. Sainani says LLMs are not ready to take over statisticians' jobs, and Nuzzo says statisticians have a growing role as the link between machines and the people using them.
Q: How can LLMs improve statistical analysis?
A: Sainani says people who analyze data on their own, sometimes blindly in Excel, can now get help from an LLM with coding in R, visualizing data, and checking for errors.
Q: Why does AI still need human oversight?
A: Sainani notes that AI can make weird, unexpected mistakes, so a person needs to think about and oversee the analysis.
Q: What do statisticians understand that machines do not?
A: Nuzzo says machines are good at automation and saving time, but they lack insight into human psychology and what people need. Statisticians understand both how the models are built, trained, and validated and how people interpret them.

items.title: TiDAR: Think in Diffusion, Talk in Autoregression (Paper Analysis)
items.summary:
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08923

Abstract:
Diffusion language models hold the promise of fast parallel generation, while autoregressive (AR) models typically excel in quality due to their causal structure aligning naturally with language modeling. This raises a fundamental question: can we achieve a synergy with high throughput, higher GPU utilization, and AR level quality? Existing methods fail to effectively balance these two aspects, either prioritizing AR using a weaker model for sequential drafting (speculative decoding), leading to lower drafting efficiency, or using some form of left-to-right (AR-like) decoding logic for diffusion, which still suffers from quality degradation and forfeits its potential parallelizability. We introduce TiDAR, a sequence-level hybrid architecture that drafts tokens (Thinking) in Diffusion and samples final outputs (Talking) AutoRegressively - all within a single forward pass using specially designed structured attention masks. This design exploits the free GPU compute density, achieving a strong balance between drafting and verification capacity. Moreover, TiDAR is designed to be serving-friendly (low overhead) as a standalone model. We extensively evaluate TiDAR against AR models, speculative decoding, and diffusion variants across generative and likelihood tasks at 1.5B and 8B scales. Thanks to the parallel drafting and sampling as well as exact KV cache support, TiDAR outperforms speculative decoding in measured throughput and surpasses diffusion models like Dream and Llada in both efficiency and quality. Most notably, TiDAR is the first architecture to close the quality gap with AR models while delivering 4.71x to 5.91x more tokens per second.

Authors: Jingyu Liu, Xin Dong, Zhifan Ye, Rishabh Mehta, Yonggan Fu, Vartika Singh, Jan Kautz, Ce Zhang, Pavlo Molchanov

items.title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time (Paper Analysis)
items.summary:
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663

Abstract:
Over more than a decade there has been an extensive research effort on how to effectively utilize recurrent models and attention. While recurrent models aim to compress the data into a fixed-size memory (called hidden state), attention allows attending to the entire context window, capturing the direct dependencies of all tokens. This more accurate modeling of dependencies, however, comes with a quadratic cost, limiting the model to a fixed-length context. We present a new neural long-term memory module that learns to memorize historical context and helps attention to attend to the current context while utilizing long past information. We show that this neural memory has the advantage of fast parallelizable training while maintaining a fast inference. From a memory perspective, we argue that attention due to its limited context but accurate dependency modeling performs as a short-term memory, while neural memory due to its ability to memorize the data, acts as a long-term, more persistent, memory. Based on these two modules, we introduce a new family of architectures, called Titans, and present three variants to address how one can effectively incorporate memory into this architecture. Our experimental results on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, genomics, and time series tasks show that Titans are more effective than Transformers and recent modern linear recurrent models. They further can effectively scale to larger than 2M context window size with higher accuracy in needle-in-haystack tasks compared to baselines.

Authors: Ali Behrouz, Peilin Zhong, Vahab Mirrokni

items.title: [Paper Analysis] On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval (Warning: Rant)
items.summary:
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21038

Abstract:
Vector embeddings have been tasked with an ever-increasing set of retrieval tasks over the years, with a nascent rise in using them for reasoning, instruction-following, coding, and more. These new benchmarks push embeddings to work for any query and any notion of relevance that could be given. While prior works have pointed out theoretical limitations of vector embeddings, there is a common assumption that these difficulties are exclusively due to unrealistic queries, and those that are not can be overcome with better training data and larger models. In this work, we demonstrate that we may encounter these theoretical limitations in realistic settings with extremely simple queries. We connect known results in learning theory, showing that the number of top-k subsets of documents capable of being returned as the result of some query is limited by the dimension of the embedding. We empirically show that this holds true even if we restrict to k=2, and directly optimize on the test set with free parameterized embeddings. We then create a realistic dataset called LIMIT that stress tests models based on these theoretical results, and observe that even state-of-the-art models fail on this dataset despite the simple nature of the task. Our work shows the limits of embedding models under the existing single vector paradigm and calls for future research to develop methods that can resolve this fundamental limitation.

Authors: Orion Weller, Michael Boratko, Iftekhar Naim, Jinhyuk Lee

items.title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance (Paper Analysis)
items.summary:
Paper: https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot

Abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically presumed to process context uniformly—that is, the model should handle the 10,000th token just as reliably as the 100th. However, in practice, this assumption does not hold. We observe that model performance varies significantly as input length changes, even on simple tasks.
In this report, we evaluate 18 LLMs, including the state-of-the-art GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, and Qwen3 models. Our results reveal that models do not use their context uniformly; instead, their performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows.

items.title: Energy-Based Transformers are Scalable Learners and Thinkers (Paper Review)
items.summary:
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02092
Code: https://github.com/alexiglad/EBT
Website: https://energy-based-transformers.github.io/

Abstract:
Inference-time computation techniques, analogous to human System 2 Thinking, have recently become popular for improving model performances. However, most existing approaches suffer from several limitations: they are modality-specific (e.g., working only in text), problem-specific (e.g., verifiable domains like math and coding), or require additional supervision/training on top of unsupervised pretraining (e.g., verifiers or verifiable rewards). In this paper, we ask the question "Is it possible to generalize these System 2 Thinking approaches, and develop models that learn to think solely from unsupervised learning?" Interestingly, we find the answer is yes, by learning to explicitly verify the compatibility between inputs and candidate-predictions, and then re-framing prediction problems as optimization with respect to this verifier. Specifically, we train Energy-Based Transformers (EBTs) -- a new class of Energy-Based Models (EBMs) -- to assign an energy value to every input and candidate-prediction pair, enabling predictions through gradient descent-based energy minimization until convergence. Across both discrete (text) and continuous (visual) modalities, we find EBTs scale faster than the dominant Transformer++ approach during training, achieving an up to 35% higher scaling rate with respect to data, batch size, parameters, FLOPs, and depth. During inference, EBTs improve performance with System 2 Thinking by 29% more than the Transformer++ on language tasks, and EBTs outperform Diffusion Transformers on image denoising while using fewer forward passes. Further, we find that EBTs achieve better results than existing models on most downstream tasks given the same or worse pretraining performance, suggesting that EBTs generalize better than existing approaches. Consequently, EBTs are a promising new paradigm for scaling both the learning and thinking capabilities of models.

Authors: Alexi Gladstone, Ganesh Nanduru, Md Mofijul Islam, Peixuan Han, Hyeonjeong Ha, Aman Chadha, Yilun Du, Heng Ji, Jundong Li, Tariq Iqbal

items.title: [GRPO Explained] DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models
items.summary:
#deepseek #llm #grpo

GRPO is one of the core advancements used in Deepseek-R1, but was introduced already last year in this paper that uses a combination of new RL techniques and iterative data collection to achieve remarkable performance on mathematics benchmarks with just a 7B model.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300

Abstract:
Mathematical reasoning poses a significant challenge for language models due to its complex and structured nature. In this paper, we introduce DeepSeekMath 7B, which continues pre-training DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B with 120B math-related tokens sourced from Common Crawl, together with natural language and code data. DeepSeekMath 7B has achieved an impressive score of 51.7% on the competition-level MATH benchmark without relying on external toolkits and voting techniques, approaching the performance level of Gemini-Ultra and GPT-4. Self-consistency over 64 samples from DeepSeekMath 7B achieves 60.9% on MATH. The mathematical reasoning capability of DeepSeekMath is attributed to two key factors: First, we harness the significant potential of publicly available web data through a meticulously engineered data selection pipeline. Second, we introduce Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), that enhances mathematical reasoning abilities while concurrently optimizing the memory usage of PPO.

Authors: Zhihong Shao, Peiyi Wang, Qihao Zhu, Runxin Xu, Junxiao Song, Xiao Bi, Haowei Zhang, Mingchuan Zhang, Y.K. Li, Y. Wu, Daya Guo
